**Ch 010 draft review:**

- "I fought my way against the storm" — source says "stubborn storm," draft says just "the storm." No confusion.
- "Shaking off the sleet, I seated myself near the door, and was surprised to see Queequeg." — Source has Queequeg introduced earlier in the book; he is an established character. No issue.
- "Yes, Ishmael, the same fate may be thine. But somehow I grew merry again." — Source context: "with what feelings...I regarded those marble tablets...read the fate of the whalemen who had gone before me. Yes, Ishmael..." The draft cuts the framing sentence. Does "Yes, Ishmael, the same fate may be thine" parse without it? The "same fate" has a broken pivot — the same fate as *whom*? The antecedent is the fate of the whalemen described in the tablets, which IS present in the draft (the tablets are quoted in full). A competent reader can connect "the same fate" to the tablet inscriptions showing whalemen who died. Not genuinely confusing.
- "A stove boat will make me an immortal by brevet." — Source: "Delightful inducements to embark, fine chance for promotion, it seems—aye, a stove boat will make me an immortal by brevet." The draft cuts the ironic setup. Is the sentence parseable? Yes, it's ironic on its own. A reader might find it slightly abrupt but not actually confused.

**Ch 011 draft review:**

- "There must be some sober reason; it must symbolize something unseen." — Source: "I pondered some time without fully comprehending the reason for this. Father Mapple enjoyed such a wide reputation for sincerity and sanctity, that I could not suspect him of courting notoriety by any mere tricks of the stage. No, thought I, there must be some sober reason..." The draft cuts the framing of Ishmael's reasoning process and the dismissal of the "mere tricks of the stage" alternative. The draft sentence opens with "There must be some sober reason" — this is a broken pivot. In the source, "sober reason" contrasts with the dismissed hypothesis (courting notoriety/stage tricks). In the draft, the reader has no idea what non-sober reason was considered and rejected. However — does a reader need that contrast to understand the sentence? The sentence "There must be some sober reason; it must symbolize something unseen" is parseable and its meaning (Ishmael is puzzling over the ladder-pulling) is clear from the preceding paragraph about dragging up the ladder. The contrast is lost but the reader isn't *confused*. Gate test: less ornamented, not confusing.

- "The wall behind the pulpit was adorned with a large painting..." — Source locates this: "Between the marble cenotaphs on either hand of the pulpit, the wall which formed its back was adorned..." The draft says "The wall behind the pulpit." The marble cenotaphs/tablets were established in Ch 010 draft. No confusion about which wall.

- "The pulpit itself bore the same sea-taste: its panelled front..." — Source: "Nor was the pulpit itself without a trace of the same sea-taste that had achieved the ladder and the picture." The draft's "the same sea-taste" refers back to the painting description. Does "the same" have a clear antecedent? In the draft, the previous paragraph described the painting but didn't use the phrase "sea-taste." So "the same sea-taste" dangles slightly — same as what? But reading the draft, a reader would understand "the same sea-taste" refers to the nautical character of the painting just described. Not genuinely confusing.

After careful review, I find no structurally damaging compressions that meet the gate test threshold. The draft chapters are coherent as abridgments.
